A token is one piece of text the model sees.","headline":{"text":"Same word, different token counts","semantic":"problem"},"tags":["Paris","spacing","capitals"]},{"beatId":"b2","narration":"So why not single characters? A paragraph becomes thousands of steps. Why not whole words? Each typo needs its own entry. Subword pieces sit between: common words take one token, rare ones several. That list is the vocabulary.","headline":{"text":"Subword pieces: the middle ground","semantic":"decision"},"tags":["characters","whole words","subword pieces"]},{"beatId":"b3","narration":"Start from raw bytes: two hundred fifty-six byte values, so nothing is ever unknown. Then a merge loop adds the most frequent neighbouring pair as a new symbol: \"t\" plus \"h\" becomes \"th\". Replace it and repeat.","headline":{"text":"Vocabulary = bytes plus learned merges","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["byte-level","merge loop","new symbol"],"statCards":[{"value":"256","label":"starting byte values","sourceRef":"num-2"}],"source":"A field guide to subword merges"},{"beatId":"b4","narration":"The merge order matters. Early merges join common pairs; late ones build whole words. Encoding replays that list, so common words become one token and rare ones stay in pieces.","headline":{"text":"Merge order decides the split","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["merge order","replay","rare words"]},{"beatId":"b5","narration":"That same word from the start. Before merges run, text is cut into chunks they never cross: pre-tokenization. A space sticks to the next word, and capitals change the pieces. \"Paris\", \" Paris\" and \"PARIS\" give one, one and three tokens.","headline":{"text":"Pre-tokenization = where merges stop","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["pre-tokenization","leading space","capitals"]},{"beatId":"b6","narration":"Corrowby bills each request by token and must fit each chat in a token-sized context window. Their English replies ran at about one point three tokens per word. A rarer language needed about three times as many.","headline":{"text":"Word counts miss the real count","semantic":"problem"},"tags":["token billing","context window"],"statCards":[{"value":"about 1.3","label":"tokens per word","sourceRef":"num-4"}],"source":"Field notes: counting tokens before you pay for them"},{"beatId":"b7","narration":"So Corrowby now counts each reply with the model's own tokenizer and budgets in tokens, per language. The Paris reply fits, and costs are visible. Count tokens, not words.","headline":{"text":"Same reply, honest budget","semantic":"resolution"},"tags":["exact tokenizer","per-language cost"]}]}
